summaries.example: Imagine sorting a toy box. You might sort toys by what they are, how many there are, where they are, or what they are doing. Philosophers ask whether the world itself has a small set of basic kinds, or whether these kinds mainly come from how people think and speak. A ball could be sorted as an object, something round, something in a room, or something being thrown. Different sorting systems can all be useful for different questions.
summaries.summary: A category is a very general way of grouping things. Philosophers have asked whether categories are built into reality, built into human thinking, or revealed by language. Aristotle tried to list the highest kinds of things. Kant instead focused on the basic concepts that make thinking about objects possible. Husserl connected kinds of meanings with kinds of possible objects and allowed more than one dimension of classification. Later philosophers proposed many different systems, including systems with one top category, several top categories, or only a few basic categories. Because these proposals disagree, some philosophers doubt that there is one complete and uniquely correct map of reality. Even so, categories remain useful. They can organize knowledge, compare theories, and expose category mistakes, such as treating a way of organizing many things as if it were just one more thing beside them.
key_ideas: Some philosophers think categories describe the basic kinds that really exist.
Others think categories describe the main ways human minds or languages organize things.
Aristotle listed broad kinds such as substance, quantity, place, action, and feeling what happens to something.
Kant looked at the basic ideas needed for people to think about objects.
Husserl studied both kinds of meanings and the possible things those meanings point to.
Many philosophers doubt that one perfect category list can be found, but category differences can still help clear up confusion.
summaries.why_it_matters: Categories affect how we describe the world and solve problems. A careful classification can show that an argument mixes unlike kinds of things. Categories are also used in language studies, thinking research, medicine, and computer systems that organize information. We do not have to believe that one list is the final truth in order to use categories thoughtfully.

important_terms.definition: A very general kind or group used to sort things, ideas, or experiences.
A planned set of categories that tries to organize many or all kinds of things.
The study of what exists and what kinds of things there are.
A mistake made by treating something as if it belonged to the wrong kind.

questions_to_think_about: Can one thing belong to different categories depending on the question?
Is a school a building, a group of people, or an organized activity?
What makes a sentence a category mistake?
Would the same category system work for every language and subject?

summaries.example: Consider the claim, “The university is next to the library.” It may sound ordinary, but “university” can mean an organized institution, while “library” may mean a building. If someone visits several colleges and offices and then asks to be shown the university as one more building, the problem may be a category mistake. The example illustrates why philosophers ask whether terms refer to objects, properties, events, relations, or structures that organize other things.
summaries.summary:
The philosophical study of categories asks how the most general kinds of things, concepts, meanings, or entities should be distinguished. In the Aristotelian realist tradition, categories are intended to describe the world's highest genera and thereby support metaphysical answers to “What is there?” Kantian conceptualism changes the target: categories are the a priori concepts that make objective cognition possible, so they concern objects as knowable rather than reality considered apart from experience. Husserlian descriptivism distinguishes categories of meaning from categories of possible objects and develops formal and material dimensions of classification. Later philosophers have offered competing realist and descriptive systems, ranging from elaborate hierarchies to very small sets of fundamental categories.

The entry emphasizes that disagreement is not merely about which labels to choose. Philosophers disagree about the proper method, whether one highest genus exists, whether a system must be exhaustive, and whether categorization should have one dimension or several. The variety of systems supports skepticism about discovering one uniquely true and complete ontology. Still, categories can be valuable as frameworks: they make assumptions explicit, prevent ad hoc comparisons, organize inquiry, and help identify category mistakes. A related approach studies category differences rather than complete systems. Ryle uses absurd substitutions to expose logical-type differences; Fregean approaches connect categories of entities with kinds of linguistic expressions and their identity conditions. Linguistics, cognitive science, and information science extend these questions into language use, human categorization, and formal knowledge organization.
key_ideas: Aristotelian realism treats a category system as an inventory of the highest kinds of beings. Aristotle's list includes substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, posture, state, action, and being acted upon.

Kant shifts the focus from reality considered independently of experience to the concepts necessary for judging and knowing possible objects. His categories are connected to forms of judgment and apply to objects of possible cognition.

Husserl distinguishes categories of meaning from categories of possible objects. He also distinguishes formal categories from material regions, so classification can proceed along more than one dimension.
Modern systems differ widely: some are realist, some descriptive, some hierarchical, and some deliberately minimal. There is no broad agreement about their number, method, or structure.

Skepticism arises because proposed systems may not be demonstrably exhaustive or uniquely correct. Mutual exclusivity and completeness are useful standards, but many different divisions can satisfy them.
Category distinctions can have practical philosophical value without settling ultimate ontology. They may diagnose paradoxes, clarify language, compare theories, and guide information systems.
summaries.why_it_matters: Category choices shape metaphysical arguments, theories of mind, accounts of language, and systems for organizing knowledge. Making those choices explicit can reveal hidden assumptions and show why an apparent problem depends on mixing unlike kinds. Even if no single ontology is established, a category framework can make inquiry more systematic and help researchers compare what different theories accept or reject.

important_terms.definition: A highest-level kind under which narrower kinds may fall; philosophers disagree about whether there is one highest kind.
A proposed classification of the most general kinds of entities, concepts, or meanings.
The philosophical study of being, existence, and the kinds of entities there are or could be.
The view that categories aim to identify real, mind-independent kinds of entities.
The view that categories primarily express the basic concepts governing human understanding.
An approach that describes categories implicit in thought, experience, or language without deciding which categories are really instantiated.
A classification error in which an expression or entity is treated as belonging to the wrong logical or conceptual kind.
A condition that determines when something counts as the same thing again, often used to distinguish kinds of objects.

questions_to_think_about: What would count as evidence that a category system is exhaustive rather than merely useful?
Does a difference in grammatical or conceptual role reveal a difference in reality, or only in our descriptions?
Can an entity be classified along several independent dimensions without creating a contradiction?
Why might identity conditions be a better guide to object-categories than intuitive resemblance?
Should “thing” or “entity” count as a single highest category if it does not provide a criterion of identity?

summaries.example: Suppose a student says, “The school is walking to the gym.” The sentence uses “school” as if it were an individual person, but “school” might mean a building, an institution, or a group of people. The sentence could be changed if the meaning is clear: “The students are walking to the gym.” Philosophers call this kind of mix-up a category mistake. It shows why we need to ask what sort of thing a word or idea is about.
summaries.summary:
Philosophers use the word category for a very general kind or type. A category system is an organized set of such kinds. One major question is whether categories describe reality itself or mainly describe the ways people think and speak. Aristotle's approach is usually understood as realist: his categories aim to identify the highest kinds of entities. Kant takes a conceptualist route, arguing that certain basic concepts are necessary for human understanding and for making objective judgments about objects. Husserl offers a more descriptive approach, distinguishing categories of meanings from categories of the possible objects those meanings can be about. He also allows classification in different dimensions, such as formal structure and material nature.

Later philosophers have suggested many systems, but their lists and methods differ greatly. Some systems have one top category and branch downward; others do not. Some claim to describe real entities, while others only describe possible categories and do not say whether anything actually belongs to them. This variety leads to skepticism about whether one complete, uniquely correct system can be discovered. Requirements such as completeness and keeping categories separate are helpful, but many classifications can meet them. Because of this, philosophers often study category differences instead. A category mistake occurs when we treat one kind of thing as another kind, as when an institution is treated like a person or a way of organizing things is treated like one more object. Such distinctions can clarify arguments, language, and knowledge systems.
key_ideas: Aristotle tried to identify the broadest kinds of things, including substances, quantities, qualities, relations, places, times, actions, and what things undergo.
Kant argued that categories are basic concepts required for making objective judgments about possible objects, rather than a direct list of reality as it is independently of experience.
Husserl separated categories of meanings from categories of objects and described formal and material ways to classify them.
Philosophers have proposed many different category systems. Some use a branching tree; others use several dimensions or only a few basic categories.
A system should ideally place everything in a category and keep categories at the same level separate, but these rules do not select one unique system.
Category differences can help explain paradoxes and philosophical confusion even when a philosopher does not claim to know every category in existence.
summaries.why_it_matters: How we sort things affects how we explain them. A good category distinction can uncover a hidden assumption, prevent a misleading comparison, or show that a puzzle began by combining unlike kinds. Categories also help organize information in areas such as language, science, medicine, and computing. Studying them teaches us to question the structure behind our descriptions.

important_terms.definition: A broad kind used to classify things, ideas, meanings, or possible objects.
A set of very general categories meant to organize a field or, sometimes, everything that exists.
The branch of philosophy that asks what exists and what kinds of things there are.
The approach that treats categories as real divisions among the highest kinds of beings.
The approach that treats categories as basic concepts used by the human mind to understand objects.
A careful description of categories found in thought, experience, or language without claiming that each category has real members.
A confusing statement or argument caused by assigning something to the wrong kind.

questions_to_think_about: Could a word fit one category in everyday speech and another in a scientific theory?
Why might a list of separate categories still fail to be the one true list?
Is “object” a useful category, or is it too general to tell us how to identify things?
How can a category mistake make a philosophical problem seem harder than it is?
